title: The King's Hares
lines: Once upon a time, beyond the seven times seven lands,
there lived a poor woman, and she had three sons.
They were as poor as church mice; they cooked with water
and stirred it with a stick, and lived from one day to the next.
The lads grew tired of this hard life, and they made up their minds
that they would go out from home somewhere,
for they could not go on like this forever and a day.
One day the eldest said to his mother:
"Mother dear, bake me a cake in the ashes,
for I am setting out to try my luck."
The poor woman baked it, and the lad set out into the wide world.
On and on he went, over hills and valleys, and came to a golden well.
He sat down beside it, took out his ash cake, and began to eat.
As he sat there eating, a little mouse ran up to him and said:
"Listen, lad, give me a bite of that cake,
for it is seven whole days since I have eaten a single bite."
"I don't care," said the lad,
"even if you have not eaten for seventy-seven days, as long as I have enough."
The little mouse crept away very sadly
and hid in a hole, and the lad went on his way.
He went and went until he came to the king's city.
He went straight to the palace, sat down by the gate, and waited for good luck.
Then all at once the king himself came out,
saw the lad, even greeted him, and asked:
"What brings you here, poor lad?"
"Your Majesty, I put my life and death in your hands;
I am looking for work, if I can find any."
The king said:
"Come in, lad. I have a hundred hares in my yard, and I give them to you.
Drive them out to the meadow, but guard them so well
that not one gets lost, or else it is the hares and your head!"
Next morning the lad drove the hundred hares out,
but as soon as they reached the meadow, the hundred ran a hundred ways.
Oh, how the lad lost heart! He did not even dare look toward the palace;
he ran away and did not stop until he got home.
At home he told where he had been and all that had happened to him.
Then the second lad stepped forward
to try his luck, and he spat on his hands hard,
saying he would guard those hundred hares, heaven knows, if it took his life.
But he did just as "well" as the eldest.
At the golden well he too sat down to eat,
and the mouse asked him too for a bite of the ash cake, but he gave it none.
Then he went on to the king's city and took service with the king,
but the first morning he drove the hares out, the hundred ran a hundred ways.
He too went home very sadly, and now the youngest lad got ready to go:
perhaps luck would be kinder to him.
His mother baked him an ash cake as big
as a big cart wheel, and with it he set out into the world.
On and on he went, and came to the golden well.
As he sat there eating, the mouse ran up and asked him very nicely
to give it, for heaven's sake, a bite of cake,
for it was fourteen whole days since it had eaten.
"Gladly, little mouse," said the lad,
"perhaps the good Lord will help me, so I won't have to live long on this cake."
The little mouse thanked him kindly and said:
"Well, poor lad, a good deed brings a good deed back!
I asked your two brothers, neither gave me anything, and the Lord helped neither."
With that it ran into its hole and came back with a little horn.
"I give you this horn," said the mouse. "Keep it, it may be useful."
"Why, what could I ever do with this?"
asked the lad.
"Just take it," said the mouse, "and whatever danger you are in,
blow it, and all that is bad will turn to good."
"Well," thought the poor lad,
"if it does no good, it does no harm. I'll take it with me."
He put it in his bag, went on, and did not stop until the king's city,
and in it, until the gate of the king's palace.
He arrived, sat down in the gateway, and soon the king came by.
"What are you looking for here, poor lad?"
asked the king.
The lad told him what he wanted: to find work in some good place.
"You have come to the right place," said the king. "I have a hundred hares,
and they need a clever herder, for I have not found one I like yet."
They shook hands at once, but the king warned the lad most strictly
that not one hare must be lost, or else it would be the hares and his head!
Very well.
Next morning the lad went out to the meadow with the hundred hares,
but before they even sniffed the grass, they ran off every which way.
"Oh, Holy Mary, Saint Joseph!" cried the lad. "What shall I do now?"
Then he remembered the horn; he pulled it out and blew it,
and the hundred hares turned at once and ran together like so many sheep.
The king saw this from the porch of the palace;
he shook his head and could not for the life of him think
what devilish trick the lad had used to gather those hares.
"Just wait," he thought, "today at least one of the hundred will be missing!
If not, I will put you to another test."
At once he ordered a servant girl to go out to the meadow with a sack
and ask the herder for a hare in the king's name.
The girl went out and asked for the hare, but the lad said
he would not give one even for heaven's sake, for his head was dear to him.
"But this and that," said the girl, "there is a feast at the house,
and the king will have both our heads off if there is no hare on the table."
As they argued like this, from who knows where
the little mouse appeared and whispered to the lad:
"Just give her one, don't be afraid, and leave the rest to me!"
The lad listened to the mouse, quickly grabbed a hare by the ears,
put it in the sack, and the girl set off with it.
That very minute the little mouse jumped up onto the sack,
and before the girl had taken a hundred steps, it chewed open the end of the sack;
the hare jumped out and ran back to the others as fast as it could go.
The mouse jumped down from the sack,
quickly picked up a big lump of cow dung and pushed it into the sack instead.
In the evening the lad went home and drove the hundred hares in at the big gate.
Out came the king to meet him, cursing so that the whole yard shook.
"Come here, come here, you good-for-nothing! What did you send me in that sack?"
The lad answered:
"May God not be my God if it was not a hare, Your Majesty."
They called the servant girl.
"Well, girl, what did the herder give you?"
"Truly, Your Majesty,
I put my life and death in your hands, he really gave me a hare."
"Hm," said the king,
"I never ate anything like that in all my life. So where is the hare now?"
They counted the hares once, twice, three times, but it always came to a hundred.
"Well, listen, poor lad," said the king,
"I never had a herder like you, who sends a hare and still has none missing.
So what do you wish for?"
"Only a tub of money, Your Majesty, for we are very poor at home."
At once the king had a great big sack of money measured out,
so big that the lad needed twelve oxen to pull it home.
And they became so very rich that people came from far lands to marvel at them.
They are still alive today, if they have not died.
